description: How class, gender, ethnicity and disability shape opportunities. Devine on the affluent worker.
content_html:
What Are Life Chances?

Life chances is a concept associated with Max Weber. It refers to the probability that a person will enjoy the positive outcomes that a society has to offer — good health, educational success, secure employment, satisfactory housing and a long life expectancy. Weber argued that class position shapes life chances because it determines a person’s position in the market. In the UK, however, life chances are not determined by class alone. Research consistently shows that gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability, religion and belief all intersect with class to shape what individuals can realistically expect from life.

Key Fact

The spec identifies seven factors affecting life chances: social class, gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability, and religion and belief. Each can independently and in combination with others shape a person’s access to education, employment, health and other valued resources.

Social Class and Life Chances

Social class remains one of the strongest predictors of life outcomes in the UK. Children from professional and managerial backgrounds are significantly more likely to attend higher-performing schools, obtain higher-education qualifications and enter well-paid occupations than those from working-class backgrounds. They tend to have better health outcomes and longer life expectancy. This is partly explained by material deprivation — working-class families may have fewer financial resources to invest in education, private healthcare or extracurricular activities. It is also explained by cultural and social capital: the values, knowledge and social networks that enable middle-class families to navigate educational systems more effectively.

Social mobility — the ability to change one’s position in the class hierarchy — is relevant here. Intergenerational mobility describes movement across generations (a working-class child reaching a professional occupation). Intragenerational mobility describes movement within a single lifetime. Functionalists see upward social mobility as evidence that the system is working meritocratically; Marxists argue that structural barriers mean mobility is limited and class position is substantially reproduced across generations.

Devine and the Affluent Worker

Fiona Devine’s study Affluent Workers Revisited (1992) directly addressed how class shapes life chances by returning to the site of an earlier study. In the 1960s, Goldthorpe and Lockwood had studied male manual workers at the Vauxhall car plant in Luton, arguing that affluent workers were becoming embourgeoisified — absorbed into middle-class values and lifestyles as wages rose. They also proposed the concept of privatised instrumentalism — social relationships focused on the home, with work valued only as a means to earn wages.

Devine revisited Luton in the late 1980s, interviewing manual workers and their wives. She did not find evidence of full embourgeoisement: workers’ lifestyles were neither as communal as traditional working-class communities nor as home-centred and privatised as Goldthorpe and Lockwood had suggested. Crucially, Devine found that her respondents retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality, even though many aspired to consumer goods and rising living standards. Many had also lost faith in the Labour Party to deliver greater equality. Devine’s study illustrates that class continues to shape attitudes, aspirations and life chances even among relatively well-paid workers.

Gender: Women in the UK continue to earn less on average than men — the gender pay gap persists across most sectors. Women are over-represented in part-time and low-paid work. Feminist sociologists link this to patriarchal structures that undervalue women’s labour and create barriers to senior positions (the “glass ceiling”). Life expectancy is longer for women, but women are more likely to experience poverty in old age due to lower pension accumulation.

Race and ethnicity: Ethnic minority groups in the UK face, on average, higher unemployment rates, lower wages, and over-representation in lower-status occupations compared with White British groups. However, outcomes vary considerably between different ethnic groups and are shaped by a combination of factors: direct discrimination, institutional racism, differences in geographic concentration, educational background and cultural capital. Sociologists are careful to explain ethnic inequalities using sociological mechanisms rather than treating ethnicity as inherently predictive of outcomes.

Age: Life chances vary across the life course. Young people may face higher unemployment and are less likely to own their own homes. Older workers, especially those over fifty, can face ageism in the labour market. Elderly people on fixed incomes may be vulnerable to poverty, and access to healthcare and social care becomes increasingly important.

Sexuality: LGBTQ+ individuals face higher rates of mental health difficulties, discrimination in employment and housing, and social exclusion in some contexts. Attitudes and legal protections have changed significantly in the UK since the 1960s, but inequalities in life chances persist.

Disability: Disabled people in the UK have significantly lower employment rates and, on average, lower incomes than non-disabled people. The disability employment gap reflects both barriers to access and employer discrimination. Social models of disability argue that these inequalities are produced by social barriers and attitudes rather than by disability itself.

Religion and belief: Religious identity can affect life chances through discrimination, social capital (religious communities can provide supportive networks) and cultural expectations around education and employment. Some religious groups are associated with higher educational attainment; others face Islamophobia or other forms of prejudice in the labour market.

Functionalists, following Davis and Moore, would argue that differential life chances reflect differential rewards for positions of varying functional importance. If some people have better life chances, this is partly because they have worked harder, trained longer or demonstrated greater talent — consistent with a meritocratic system. Social mobility is evidence the system is working.

Marxists argue that life chances are shaped fundamentally by class position, which is determined by ownership of the means of production. Material deprivation, restricted access to education and the reproduction of ruling-class ideology all ensure that class inequality in life chances is reproduced across generations. The system is not meritocratic but serves the interests of the bourgeoisie.

Feminist sociologists argue that patriarchy creates systematic inequalities in life chances for women across all class positions. Even women in professional occupations face the gender pay gap and the glass ceiling. Walby’s framework of six structures of patriarchy (developed further in Lesson 6) helps explain why gender inequality in life chances persists despite formal legal equality.

Key Fact

Devine’s 1992 study found that affluent workers had NOT become embourgeoisified: they retained class identities, resented extreme inequality, and had not become as privatised and home-centred as the earlier Goldthorpe and Lockwood study had suggested.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe question on factors affecting life chances, avoid listing all seven factors without developing any. The mark scheme rewards depth, not breadth. Choose two or three factors and describe how each affects life chances using sociological vocabulary: material deprivation, glass ceiling, ageism, institutional racism, patriarchy. On a 12-mark Discuss, make sure you compare perspectives — if the question is about class and life chances, a Mastering answer will contrast the functionalist view (meritocratic rewards) with the Marxist view (structural reproduction of inequality) and name Devine’s study as evidence about working-class aspirations and class identity.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Life chances — the probability of enjoying positive outcomes such as education, health and employment — are shaped by class, gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability, and religion and belief, often in combination.
  • Devine’s 1992 study revisiting Luton found that affluent workers had not become embourgeoisified: they retained class identities and resentment at inequality, challenging the privatised instrumentalism thesis of Goldthorpe and Lockwood.
  • Functionalists see differential life chances as meritocratic; Marxists argue they reflect structural class reproduction; feminists argue patriarchy independently shapes women’s life chances regardless of class position.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist revisited the Luton car plant workers in the early 1990s to study the life chances of affluent workers?
A) Goldthorpe
B) Townsend
C) Devine
D) Murray

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that life chances refer to the opportunities available to an individual; 1 mark for linking this to social position or structural factors (e.g. 'Life chances are the opportunities an individual has to improve their quality of life, such as access to education, health and housing, shaped by their position in the social structure including their class, gender and ethnicity.').

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way that gender affects life chances in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying one way gender affects life chances (e.g. the gender pay gap; over-representation of women in low-paid part-time work; the glass ceiling; women's greater likelihood of poverty in old age). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Women in the UK earn less on average than men in the same or comparable occupations, a pattern described as the gender pay gap. This affects their overall financial security, pension accumulation and economic independence over the life course. Feminist sociologists link this to patriarchal structures that undervalue women's labour and create barriers to senior positions rather than to differences in ability or effort.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Devine's key findings from her study of affluent workers in Luton.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Devine revisited Luton in the late 1980s, interviewing workers and their wives (1 mark). She did not find evidence to support embourgeoisement or full privatised instrumentalism (1 mark). Workers retained class identities and resentment at extreme inequality despite rising living standards and consumer aspirations (1 mark). Many had lost faith in the Labour Party as a vehicle for change, but had not abandoned working-class values in the way Goldthorpe and Lockwood's earlier study had implied (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way that ethnicity affects life chances in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying one way (e.g. higher unemployment rates among some ethnic minority groups; lower average wages; over-representation in lower-status occupations; experience of institutional racism). 2 marks for a developed description that uses sociological vocabulary and explains a mechanism rather than merely stating a correlation: e.g. 'Some ethnic minority groups in the UK face higher unemployment rates than White British groups. Sociologists explain this through direct discrimination in hiring, institutional racism in organisations, and barriers related to social capital networks. This means ethnic inequality in employment is not explained by individual ability but by structural patterns of discrimination.'

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that social class is the most important factor shaping life chances in modern Britain. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments. Class as a factor is explained in depth (material deprivation, social mobility, Devine's findings on class identity and life aspirations). At least one other factor is developed as a serious alternative or complementary explanation (gender — feminist perspective; ethnicity — structural/institutional racism argument). Functionalist perspective acknowledges differential life chances but attributes them to meritocratic reward structures. A supported judgement addresses whether class is the most important single factor or whether intersecting factors offer a more complete explanation.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present with named sociologists; judgement offered but development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant but mostly one-sided or underdeveloped; some sociological vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic factual points, few named theorists, little evaluation or judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What concept did Goldthorpe and Lockwood use to describe a working-class lifestyle centred on the home, with work valued only as a means to earn money?
Which sociologist's 1992 study found that affluent Luton car workers had NOT become embourgeoisified?
The ability to move up or down the social hierarchy is called social _____.
_____ mobility describes movement between class positions across generations, for example a working-class child becoming a professional.
Match each factor to a key life chances issue it creates:
right: Gender pay gap and over-representation in low-paid, part-time work
Ageism in the labour market and poverty risk in old age
Significant employment gap and lower average incomes compared to non-disabled people

flashcard_questions.a: The opportunities to improve quality of life — education, health, employment, housing — shaped by social position.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sociologist first used the concept of life chances in relation to class?

flashcard_questions.a: The theory that affluent workers adopt middle-class values and lifestyles as their wages rise.
A working-class lifestyle centred on home and family, with work valued only as a means to earn wages.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Devine find when she revisited the Luton car workers in the early 1990s?
flashcard_questions.a: Workers retained class identities and resentment at inequality; embourgeoisement had not occurred.
Movement between class positions across generations, such as a working-class child entering a professional occupation.
Movement between class positions within a single person's own lifetime.
A lack of the material resources — income, housing, services — needed to participate fully in society.
Prejudice or discrimination on the grounds of a person's age.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one factor — other than class — that affects life chances and explain why.
flashcard_questions.a: Gender: women face a pay gap and are over-represented in low-paid work, reducing their financial security and social mobility.
An invisible barrier preventing women and minorities from advancing to senior positions in organisations.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Marxist perspective explain differential life chances?
flashcard_questions.a: Class position, determined by ownership of the means of production, shapes access to resources and reproduces inequality across generations.

glossary_terms.definition: The opportunities an individual has to improve their quality of life, including access to education, health, income and housing, shaped by their social position.
The ability to move up or down the social hierarchy, either across generations (intergenerational) or within a single lifetime (intragenerational).
Social mobility that occurs between generations, such as a child achieving a higher class position than their parents.
Social mobility that occurs within a person's own lifetime.
A lack of the material resources needed to participate fully in society, including income, housing and access to services.
The process by which the working class is said to adopt the attitudes, values and lifestyle of the middle class as their incomes rise.
A term used by Goldthorpe and Lockwood to describe a working-class lifestyle centred on the home and family, with work valued only as a means to earn wages.
Prejudice or discrimination on the grounds of a person's age.

hero_image_caption: Life chances are shaped by class, gender, ethnicity, age and other social factors that determine access to education, health and employment.
